quote: The evolutionary reasons for this are so obvious as to be worth belaboring: In the ancestral environment, politics was a matter of life and death.
content: Identity-protective cognition is the proximate mechanism, and coalitional adaptation is the ultimate explanation for why it exists. They are two levels of one account, not rivals. The ancestral story also predicts Kahan's result, the opposite of what Fable says it predicts. If reasoning evolved partly to win arguments for one's side, then ability serves the side and more ability produces more polarization. That is the argumentative theory of reasoning, which grounds reasoning in exactly this ancestral politics (Mercier & Sperber 2011). The coalitional machinery has also been shown directly: people's minds automatically encode who is allied with whom, and that encoding can be redirected by cues of alliance (Kurzban, Tooby & Cosmides 2001). The "obvious" story is the one the evidence points to.

quote: People who would be level-headed about evenhandedly weighing all sides of an issue in their professional life as scientists, can suddenly turn into slogan-chanting zombies
content: Deliberative polls are engineered to remove the conditions the essay describes: party labels, public commitment, audiences to perform for. That opinion changes under engineered conditions shows that the mind-killing has a cause which can be removed. It does not show that politics as practised is level-headed. When the partisan cue is put back, the zombie comes back, and not only online. Liberal and conservative subjects evaluated the same welfare policy according to which party was said to endorse it, and reported that the label had not influenced them (Cohen 2003). Levendusky's result, that priming a shared identity reduces polarization, also shows that the identity switch is doing the work. That is the essay's thesis.

quote: Probably because the author just couldn’t resist getting in a good, solid dig at those hated Greens.
content: The attribution of motive is a guess, and the essay flags it with "probably." It should have been left out. The advice does not depend on it. The essay's rule, "Meaning does not excuse impact," applies whatever Reiter and Criscuolo intended: an example built on "All Republicans are not pacifists" puts a party-political generalization into a logic lecture, and some readers will register that before they register defaults. Fable's own defence, that the example works because Nixon is vivid, concedes the mechanism: vivid political figures bring vivid political feelings. A neutral pair (Tweety the penguin, the standard non-political default case in the same literature) teaches the same logic without them.

quote: it’s a terrible domain in which to learn rationality, or discuss rationality, unless all the discussants are already rational
content: The essay's claim concerns the classroom, not the field: politics is "an important domain to which we should individually apply our rationality," but a terrible one "in which to learn rationality." The evidence on learning under identity threat supports that ordering. Removing the threat to self-image through self-affirmation made partisans markedly more open to counter-attitudinal evidence (Cohen, Aronson & Steele 2000). A skill is learned where the threat is low and then carried to where it is high. Morewedge's training worked in exactly that way: it taught the biases with neutral scenarios and then tested them on different problems (Morewedge et al. 2015). Louis XVI is the neutral practice case, and the minimum wage is where the skill is then used.
